hero.name: Neha
hero.who: a homemaker in Ranchi trying to get her family off their phones at dinner

story.b: Every night at nine, Neha serves dinner in their flat in Ranchi: rotis, sabzi, dal and, on good days, her husband's favourite litti. And every night four heads are bent over four phones. Her husband reads cricket news. Her son Rudra, fifteen, watches gaming videos. Her daughter Mitali texts friends. Even Neha checks the family group between bites. She has given lectures, made rules, and once hid the phones in the rice drum, which ended in a fight. Each time things improve for two days, then slide back. Her mother-in-law, visiting from Hazaribagh, remarks that the family eats together but talks like strangers. Neha agrees, and she feels tired of trying.

ask.q: Neha's lectures and strict rules keep failing after two days. What should she focus on first?
o: Make the punishment harsher, so the rule finally sticks
Understand why change is hard for them and make it easier, not just demand it
Give up, since teenagers never change their phone habits
ask.why: Harsher rules may work briefly but usually spark resistance and fights, as the hidden phones showed. Giving up ignores that change is possible. When change keeps failing, it often needs clearer direction, real motivation and an easier path, not more pressure.

chapters.take: When change keeps failing, make it easier instead of pushing harder.

story.b: Neha decides to talk instead of lecture. One afternoon she asks Rudra, gently, why he needs his phone at dinner. His answer surprises her. He agrees it is rude, and he even says he would like to stop. But his friends plan their games in the evening chat, and if he is away for an hour, he feels left out. Neha realises there are two sides in him. One side knows what is right and can make plans. The other, much stronger side runs on feelings, and it is scared of being left behind. Her lectures only ever spoke to the planner. So that night she offers a clear plan, and one for his feelings too: tell his friends he is offline from nine to nine-thirty.

ask.q: Neha's husband knows he should walk daily but never does. What does the idea of a thinking side and a feeling side suggest?
o: He needs only a clearer plan, since he already knows walking is good
He needs only a scare, so a frightening article about heart disease will do
He needs both a clear plan and something that makes him want to go
ask.why: Knowing walking is good is the thinking side's job, and he already has that. A scary article may stir his feelings for a day, but without a clear plan it fades. Lasting change needs both a specific direction and a feeling that pulls him toward it.

chapters.take: Change needs both a clear plan for the mind and real feeling for the heart.

story.b: Instead of studying the bad dinners, Neha looks for good ones. She finds one quickly. On Sunday mornings, when the family makes aloo parathas together, nobody touches a phone. Her husband rolls, Mitali stuffs, and Rudra flips them on the tawa and argues about who makes the roundest one. Why does it work? Everyone has a job, the kitchen is noisy and fun, and the phones are charging in the bedroom. Neha decides to copy what already works. She gives everyone a small dinner job: Rudra sets the plates, Mitali makes the salad, her husband serves. And on Sunday night she leaves the phones charging in the bedroom too, just to see what happens.

ask.q: Neha's friend Rinku says her son studies well only on some days. How should she start fixing the bad days?
o: Study his good days closely and copy what made them work
List every bad day and talk to him about each one
Hire a strict tutor to watch him every evening
ask.why: Studying only failures tends to produce blame, not answers, and a strict tutor adds pressure without knowing what works for him. His good days already hold the answer, maybe a certain time, place or friend. Finding and copying those bright spots is faster and kinder.

chapters.take: Look for what is already working, then do more of it.

story.b: Neha notices that less phone time is too fuzzy. Everyone agrees with it, and nobody knows what it means. Does a quick look count? What about a news alert? So she spells out one clear move. When she says the dal is ready, every phone goes into the old steel basket on top of the fridge until the last plate is washed. That is the whole rule. Nobody needs to decide anything in the moment. On the first night Rudra asks if the rule covers checking the time. Neha points at the wall clock. Everyone laughs, and the phones go in the basket. The fights drop, because now there is nothing left to argue about.

ask.q: Mitali wants to be healthier this term. Which goal is most likely to change what she actually does?
o: Be healthier and more active from now on
Walk to the bus stop instead of taking the auto on school days
Try to cut down on everything unhealthy this term
ask.why: Be healthier and cut down on everything sound good, but they leave her to decide what to do in every moment, which is tiring and easy to dodge. Walking to the bus stop is one clear, concrete action she can take tomorrow, so she is far more likely to do it.

chapters.take: Spell out the exact first move. Vague goals leave people guessing.

story.h: Just to the end of the lane
story.b: Encouraged, Neha wants more: a family walk after dinner. When she proposes an hour around the lake, everyone groans. Too big. So she shrinks it. Just to the end of the lane and back, ten minutes, only on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Rudra agrees because it is shorter than one gaming video. She also prints an old photo of the four of them laughing on a walk near Kanke Dam when the children were small, and sticks it on the fridge. Nobody says much about it. But on the first Saturday, Mitali is the one who reminds everyone. By the third week, the ten minutes have stretched to twenty on their own, because someone always has a story to finish.

ask.q: Rudra has to revise a whole syllabus for his board exams and keeps avoiding it. What would help him start?
o: Make a timetable covering the entire syllabus in one go
Wait until exam pressure builds and pushes him to study
Start with one small chapter today to get an early win
ask.why: A giant timetable looks impressive but feels scary, so he keeps avoiding it, and waiting for pressure leaves too little time. One small chapter today is easy to begin, and finishing it gives a quick win. Early wins build confidence, and confidence keeps him going.

chapters.take: Make the change feel small enough to start, and let early wins carry you.

story.b: Neha notices that even with the basket, phones creep back after dinner, because everyone charges them beside their beds. So she changes the house rather than the people. She moves the charging point to the hall, next to the steel basket. She leaves the old carrom board on the dining table after dinner, with the coins already set. The TV remote goes into a drawer. She also notices that people copy each other. When the Sinha family next door start joining the lane walk, Rudra walks faster to keep up with their son. Soon two more families from the building join on Saturdays. Nobody has to be convinced. The easy path in the house now leads away from the phones.

ask.q: Neha's husband wants to stop eating fried namkeen late at night but keeps reaching for it. Which change will work best?
o: Keep the namkeen in the store room and a jar of roasted chana on the table
Rely on willpower and remind himself each night to resist
Throw everything out once and vow never to buy snacks again
ask.why: Willpower is weakest late at night, so reminders rarely hold, and a dramatic ban often ends in a binge. Changing the kitchen, so the lighter snack is easy and the fried one is hard to reach, makes the better choice the default without a nightly fight.

chapters.take: Change the surroundings, and behaviour often follows on its own.

story.h: Dinner at nine, two months on
story.b: Two months later, dinner at nine still begins with a small sound: four phones dropping into the steel basket on the fridge. Rudra sets the plates. Mitali makes the salad and complains about the onions. Her husband serves and, most nights, tells a story from his office. After dinner the carrom board comes out on some nights, and on Wednesdays and Saturdays the lane walk now has six families. Rudra's revision is on track, one chapter at a time. When Neha's mother-in-law visits again, she watches the family argue happily over a carrom shot and says nothing. Later she quietly asks Neha how she did it. Neha says she stopped pushing and started making it easy.

chapters.take: Lasting change comes from clear steps, real feelings and an easier path.
